purpose: Presentation-only teaching layer for the Hays Botany visual learner. Canonical taxonomy/range/morphology remains in content/taxa.

simple.label: Simple
simple.description: Recognize the plant using a few high-value field cues.

terms.label: Learn Terms
terms.description: Learn the botanical vocabulary while looking at the structure it names.
terms.mantra: See it → name it → use it.

field.label: Field Botany
field.description: Use technical morphology, family structure, range evidence, and comparisons.

Asteraceae.plain_signature: What looks like one flower is usually a whole flower head made of many tiny florets.
Asteraceae.look_here_first: Turn the flower head sideways. Inspect the green bracts underneath—the phyllaries—and notice whether the head has ray florets, disc florets, or both.
Asteraceae.field_signature: A capitulum of many florets on a receptacle, subtended by an involucre of phyllaries; fruit is a cypsela, often with a pappus.
Asteraceae.field_question: Before looking at flower color, what do the phyllaries and floret types look like?
Asteraceae.caveat: Asteraceae is extremely diverse. Not every member has showy ray florets.

Apocynaceae.plain_signature: For the milkweeds in this learner, leaf arrangement, sap, and the strange central flower structure do most of the work.
Apocynaceae.look_here_first: Check leaf arrangement and sap first, then look closely at the corona and gynostegium in the flower center.
Apocynaceae.field_signature: Current project emphasis is Asclepias: umbel-like clusters, a corona of five hoods, and a gynostegium containing the pollination apparatus.
Apocynaceae.field_question: Are the leaves alternate, opposite, or whorled—and what do the hoods and horns do?
Apocynaceae.caveat: These cues are strongest for the Asclepias set currently curated, not every member of Apocynaceae.

Convolvulaceae.plain_signature: Many local members are vines with a funnel-shaped fused corolla, but the leaves, sepals, hairs, and fruit often separate the species.
Convolvulaceae.look_here_first: Do not stop at the flower. Check leaf shape, hairiness, sepals, and whether the plant twines or trails.
Convolvulaceae.field_signature: Usually alternate leaves and a sympetalous, often funnelform corolla; fruit commonly a capsule. Calyx and vegetative characters are often diagnostic.
Convolvulaceae.field_question: What do the leaves and sepals look like when the flower is ignored?
Convolvulaceae.caveat: Growth habit and flower shape vary; use several characters together.

Fagaceae.plain_signature: For the oaks in this learner, the acorn, its cup, the leaves, twigs, buds, and bark are far more useful than the flowers.
Fagaceae.look_here_first: Start with a mature leaf, then check the twig/bud and the acorn cup if fruit is present.
Fagaceae.field_signature: Woody plants with nut fruits associated with a cupule; in Quercus the fruit is the acorn.
Fagaceae.field_question: What is the leaf surface like, and how much of the acorn is enclosed by the cupule?
Fagaceae.caveat: Leaf shape can vary on one tree. Use mature leaves plus twigs, buds, bark, and acorns.

Papaveraceae.plain_signature: Showy flowers and capsules are common. In the prickly poppies here, latex and prickles are high-value clues.
Papaveraceae.look_here_first: For Argemone, check latex color, prickles, sepal horns, and the fruit capsule—not flower color alone.
Papaveraceae.field_signature: Flowers commonly have separate petals and numerous stamens; ovary superior and fruit often a capsule. Latex is frequent in the family.
Papaveraceae.field_question: What color is the latex, and where are the prickles?
Papaveraceae.caveat: The learner currently emphasizes Argemone, so some cues are genus-specific.

asclepias-tuberosa.standout: A major milkweed exception in this set: the sap is clear/watery rather than milky.
asclepias-tuberosa.family_connection: It still has the specialized milkweed flower architecture—corona, hoods, and gynostegium.

asclepias-verticillata.standout: The needle-thin leaves are arranged in obvious whorls around the stem.
asclepias-verticillata.family_connection: Leaf phyllotaxy narrows the milkweeds quickly before you even inspect the flower.

asclepias-viridis.standout: The broad leaves plus green flowers and hood structure make this milkweed distinctive.
asclepias-viridis.family_connection: The corona and gynostegium are still the high-value milkweed structures.

helianthus-maximiliani.standout: Look for the tall perennial colony with many narrow, often drooping leaves.
helianthus-maximiliani.family_connection: Then confirm Asteraceae structure at the head: phyllaries outside, florets packed on the receptacle.

helianthus-annuus.standout: Usually broader leaves and more branching than Maximilian sunflower.
helianthus-annuus.family_connection: Use the involucre and phyllaries to move beyond the generic 'yellow sunflower' impression.

argemone-albiflora-subsp-texana.standout: Do not rely on white petals alone—latex, sepal horns, leaf prickles, and capsule prickles matter more.
argemone-albiflora-subsp-texana.family_connection: The showy petals and many stamens fit the poppy-family pattern, while the prickly vegetative parts help at species level.

phyllotaxy.plain: The pattern of leaves around a stem.
phyllotaxy.formal: The arrangement of leaves on an axis.
phyllotaxy.where: Trace one stem and look at where successive leaves attach.
phyllotaxy.why: Alternate, opposite, and whorled leaves can immediately narrow an ID.

alternate.plain: One leaf per node, switching sides as you move up the stem.
alternate.formal: A phyllotactic pattern with a single leaf at each node.
alternate.where: Follow the stem node by node.
alternate.why: A fast vegetative character that often separates close relatives.

opposite.plain: Two leaves emerge from the same node on opposite sides.
opposite.formal: A phyllotactic pattern with paired leaves at each node.
opposite.where: Look for leaf pairs sharing one level on the stem.
opposite.why: Useful before flowers or fruit are present.

whorled.plain: Three or more leaves emerge around the stem at one node.
whorled.formal: A phyllotactic pattern with three or more appendages at a node.
whorled.where: Look straight at a node and count the leaves radiating from it.
whorled.why: Very distinctive in plants such as whorled milkweeds.

petiole.plain: The little stalk connecting a leaf blade to the stem.
petiole.formal: The stalk attaching a leaf blade to the stem.
petiole.where: Look between the blade base and the stem.
petiole.why: Presence, absence, length, and hairiness can be diagnostic.

sessile.where: Check whether the leaf blade meets the stem directly.

pubescent.formal: Bearing trichomes or hairs on a plant surface.
pubescent.where: Use side light on leaves, stems, buds, or fruit.
pubescent.why: Hair density, position, and texture are often diagnostic.

glabrous.where: Check leaf surfaces, stems, buds, and fruit under side light.
glabrous.why: The contrast with pubescent surfaces can separate species.

lanceolate.plain: Longer than wide, widest below the middle, tapering toward the tip.
lanceolate.formal: Lance-shaped; narrowly ovate with the widest portion below the midpoint.
lanceolate.where: Look at a mature, undamaged leaf.
lanceolate.why: Leaf shape is useful when combined with arrangement and surface characters.

ovate.plain: Egg-shaped, with the broader end toward the base.
ovate.formal: Broadly egg-shaped in outline, widest below the middle.
ovate.where: Use a mature leaf and compare width from base to tip.
ovate.why: A common leaf-shape term used in keys.

rhizome.plain: A horizontal underground stem that can send up new shoots.
rhizome.formal: A usually horizontal subterranean stem bearing nodes, buds, and roots.
rhizome.where: Look at how shoots form colonies; do not excavate unnecessarily.
rhizome.why: Explains perennial colony-forming growth such as Maximilian sunflower.

capitulum.plain: The 'one flower' in a sunflower is actually a packed head of many tiny flowers.
capitulum.formal: A compact inflorescence of sessile florets on a common receptacle.
capitulum.where: Look at the whole composite head.
capitulum.why: Recognizing the capitulum is the first big step in learning Asteraceae.

phyllary.plain: One of the green bracts wrapping the base of a sunflower-family flower head.
phyllary.formal: A modified bract forming part of the involucre beneath a capitulum.
phyllary.where: Turn the head sideways and look directly underneath the florets.
phyllary.why: Shape, number of rows, texture, and tip orientation can separate similar Asteraceae.

involucre.plain: The whole ring or set of phyllaries around the base of a flower head.
involucre.formal: A whorl or series of bracts subtending an inflorescence.
involucre.where: Look at the outside/base of an Asteraceae head.
involucre.why: Its architecture is often more diagnostic than petal color.

ray-floret.plain: A small flower with a strap-like blade that looks like a petal.
ray-floret.formal: A zygomorphic floret with an expanded ligulate corolla, often at the margin of an Asteraceae head.
ray-floret.where: Look around the outer edge of a daisy-like head.
ray-floret.why: Presence, absence, number, and color can help identify genera and species.

disc-floret.plain: One of the tiny tubular flowers packed into the center of many Asteraceae heads.
disc-floret.formal: A usually actinomorphic tubular floret of the disc portion of a capitulum.
disc-floret.where: Look closely at the center of a sunflower-like head.
disc-floret.why: Disc-floret structure and color can be useful characters.

receptacle.plain: The platform the tiny florets sit on.
receptacle.formal: The expanded axis bearing floral organs or, in Asteraceae, the florets of the capitulum.
receptacle.where: In a composite head, it is underneath the florets.
receptacle.why: Whether it bears scales or paleae can help identify Asteraceae.

pappus.plain: The bristles, scales, or awns attached to the fruit in many Asteraceae.
pappus.formal: A modified calyx borne at the apex of an Asteraceae cypsela.
pappus.why: Pappus form is often important in keys.

cypsela.plain: The dry one-seeded fruit produced by an Asteraceae floret.
cypsela.formal: A dry indehiscent one-seeded fruit derived from an inferior ovary.
cypsela.where: Look at mature Asteraceae fruits below the pappus.
cypsela.why: Fruit shape and pappus characters often confirm difficult IDs.

latex.plain: Plant sap that may be milky, clear, colored, or sticky.
latex.formal: A complex cellular exudate produced in laticifers.
latex.where: Only observe from existing damage when possible; avoid injuring plants unnecessarily.
latex.why: Sap type can be extremely diagnostic in milkweeds and prickly poppies.

umbel.plain: A flower cluster whose stalks spread from about the same point, like umbrella ribs.
umbel.formal: An inflorescence with pedicels arising from a common point.
umbel.where: Look at the architecture of the entire flower cluster.
umbel.why: Milkweed clusters are commonly described as umbel-like.

corona.plain: An extra crown-like floral structure inside the corolla; in milkweeds it includes the five hoods.
corona.formal: An appendage or series of appendages between the corolla and stamens.
corona.where: Look in the center of a milkweed flower around the reproductive column.
corona.why: Its hood and horn structure is highly diagnostic in Asclepias.

gynostegium.plain: The fused central reproductive column of a milkweed flower.
gynostegium.formal: A reproductive complex formed by fusion/close union of anthers with the stigmatic head.
gynostegium.where: Look at the very center of a milkweed flower, inside the corona.
gynostegium.why: Its slits and associated pollinia are central to milkweed identification and pollination.

hood.plain: One of the five cup- or hood-shaped parts of a milkweed corona.
hood.formal: A cucullate corona segment in Asclepias, often associated with an internal horn.
hood.where: Look around the gynostegium in the flower center.
hood.why: Hood length, shape, and relation to the column help separate milkweed species.

horn.plain: A narrow projection that may rise from inside a milkweed hood.
horn.formal: A cornu arising from the interior of a corona hood in many Asclepias.
horn.where: Look into each hood from above or from the side.
horn.why: Presence, absence, and length of horns can be decisive.

pollinium.plain: A whole packet of pollen moved as one unit.
pollinium.formal: A coherent mass of pollen grains transferred together during pollination.
pollinium.where: In milkweeds, pollinia are connected to a central clip-like corpusculum.
pollinium.why: Understanding pollinia explains the unusual milkweed flower structure.

follicle.plain: A dry fruit that splits open along one side; milkweed pods are follicles.
follicle.formal: A dry dehiscent fruit derived from one carpel and opening along a single suture.
follicle.where: Look at mature milkweed fruits after flowering.
follicle.why: Fruit shape and surface can support identification.

cupule.plain: The cup or cap surrounding the base of an acorn.
cupule.formal: A cup-like involucre of fused/bract-derived structures subtending or enclosing a nut.
cupule.where: Inspect the acorn base and the scales on the cup.
cupule.why: Cup depth, shape, and scale characters help separate oaks.

catkin.plain: A dangling cluster of many tiny, usually unshowy flowers.
catkin.formal: A usually pendent spike-like inflorescence of small unisexual flowers.
catkin.where: Look for hanging flower clusters on oaks in season.
catkin.why: Useful for understanding oak reproduction, though often weaker for species-level ID.

cyathium.plain: A tiny cup-like Euphorbia structure that looks like one flower but contains highly reduced male and female flowers.
cyathium.formal: A specialized pseudanthium with a central female flower and reduced male flowers enclosed by an involucre with glands.
cyathium.where: Use a macro view of a Euphorbia flower-like unit.
cyathium.why: Recognizing the cyathium unlocks Euphorbia morphology.

corolla.plain: All the petals of a flower considered together.
corolla.formal: The inner, usually showy whorl of the perianth, composed of petals.
corolla.why: Fusion, shape, lobing, and symmetry are common family-level characters.

calyx.plain: All the sepals together—the outer floral covering below the petals.
calyx.formal: The outer whorl of the perianth, composed of sepals.
calyx.where: Look directly below or outside the corolla.
calyx.why: Sepal shape and surface are important in morning-glories and many other groups.

sepal.plain: One individual part of the calyx.
sepal.formal: A member of the outer perianth whorl.
sepal.why: Shape, length, horns, hairs, and persistence can be diagnostic.

sympetalous.plain: Petals are fused together for at least part of their length.
sympetalous.formal: Having connate petals forming a corolla tube.
sympetalous.where: Look for a continuous corolla tube rather than separate petals.
sympetalous.why: The funnel-shaped fused corolla is a strong clue in many Convolvulaceae.

capsule.plain: A dry fruit that opens to release seeds.
capsule.formal: A dry dehiscent fruit derived from a compound ovary.
capsule.where: Look at mature fruit after petals fall.
capsule.why: Opening pattern, prickles, and shape can be diagnostic.
